system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2173-12-11 05:11:00 to 2173-12-18 16:11:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted with severe epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back and nausea, consistent with an acute flare. She was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, analgesia, and antiemetics. Her course was complicated by aspiration pneumonia, diagnosed on chest X-ray, and treated with a six-day course of levofloxacin and metronidazole. Due to persistent pain with oral intake, TPN was initiated via a left basilic vein PICC line placed on hospital day 6. Her symptoms improved with TPN, and she was discharged home with ongoing TPN, strict NPO status aside from sips and medications, and plans for outpatient follow-up with GI and PCP. Weekly lab monitoring was arranged.
problems: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus
Body Mass Index less than 19, adult

procedures.long_title: Parenteral infusion of concentrated nutritional substances

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I see you came in with epigastric pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this pain under my ribs for about five days now. It goes straight through to my back. I’ve been vomiting, but nothing bloody. It feels just like my usual flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you have chronic pancreatitis, correct? You mentioned you’re on TPN at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I get these episodes a few times a year. I’ve been on TPN for a while now. My last GI visit was months ago, but I missed a few appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for that. We’ll manage this as a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. We’ll keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth except meds—and give you nutrition through your PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t eat or drink anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We need to let your pancreas rest. You’ll get all your nutrition through the TPN, which we’ll start today. We’ll also control your pain and nausea with IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My pain is pretty bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll order some IV Dilaudid for you. We’ll give it every few hours as needed. We also have Zofran for nausea. How’s your mood been lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been okay. I’m on sertraline and bupropion. I’ve been feeling down sometimes, but not worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, we’ll keep those going. Also, I noticed you have GERD. Are you having heartburn?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a little. I’ve been taking pantoprazole and ranitidine, but it still flares up sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep both those meds and add Maalox as needed. We also saw on the chest X-ray that your PICC line is in good position. No free air, so no sign of a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs came back. Your lipase is normal, which can happen in chronic pancreatitis. Liver tests are fine, and no infection signs. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still feel like I’m having a flare. Is that possible even with a normal lipase?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. The pain pattern and your history make this consistent with a flare. Lipase can be normal in chronic cases. We’re treating based on your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I was confused by that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your TPN infusion. The nutrition team recommends this to support you while your gut rests. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I remember last time I was on TPN, I had some issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your labs closely. TPN is generally safe when managed well. We’re also checking your vitamin levels—B12, zinc, copper—since long-term TPN can affect those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think my B12 was low before. I’m not taking supplements now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your B12 came back borderline low. We’re starting you on daily B12 pills. We’ll see about iron later, but for now, we’re focusing on your pancreas flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep the TPN going and adjust pain meds as needed. Your CBC is stable, so no signs of worsening anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving, and labs are stable. We’re going to keep the same plan for another day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try sipping water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to be sure your pancreas is calm. Maybe in a day or two. We’re also waiting on some vitamin results—thiamine, zinc, copper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your pain is much better. We’re going to try starting clear liquids today: water, broth, apple juice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I have tea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, plain tea is okay. Start slowly—small sips. If you tolerate it, we’ll keep advancing. We’ll also switch your pain meds to oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need IV meds anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll keep IV Zofran available if nausea returns, but you’ll take Zofran by mouth as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well on clear liquids. No pain, no vomiting. We’ll keep advancing your diet tomorrow—maybe soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper it off as you eat more. You’ll need a plan for stopping TPN at home, which we’ll discuss with GI and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed you mentioned ear fullness. Let me take a look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my right ear feels clogged. I tried cleaning it with a wire, but it didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have impacted earwax. Please don’t use wires—it can push it deeper or damage your ear. We’ll give you Debrox drops and recommend follow-up with your PCP or ENT to have it removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I didn’t know that could be harmful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re starting you on a soft diet—applesauce, toast, yogurt. How’s your GERD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some burning, but Maalox helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep both your regular meds—pantoprazole and ranitidine. Avoid spicy or fatty foods, which can trigger reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show mild anemia, but stable. Your B12 is now being supplemented. We’ll recommend iron as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I start iron now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait. Your stomach is still sensitive. Your PCP can start it later with instructions to take it with food to avoid upset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’re tolerating food, pain is minimal, and you’re back on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop it today. You’ll need a follow-up with Dr. ___ to decide if you can discontinue it completely or need adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed a few appointments. I’ll make sure to go this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That would be very helpful. They’ll also review your vitamin labs and adjust your nutrition plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your pain is mild, you’re eating well, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds should I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual meds: bupropion, sertraline, pantoprazole, ranitidine, oxybutynin, and the fentanyl patch. Also, new B12 pills daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have Dilaudid and acetaminophen for pain, and Zofran or promethazine for nausea. Use them as needed. Also, Maalox for reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor soon to discuss long-term pancreatitis management and TPN discontinuation. Also, get your vitamin labs checked—thiamine, zinc, copper—and follow up with your PCP or ENT for your ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Stay hydrated, take your meds, and keep those follow-ups. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Just confirming your discharge instructions. You’re to continue all home meds, including the new B12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve got the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember: no ear cleaning with objects. Use Debrox and see your doctor for removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll send all your records to your providers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check. Pain level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 2 now, only with deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. You’re safe to go home with services as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care and follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a reminder: if you develop severe pain, vomiting, or fever, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve been through this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge summary is ready. You’re cleared to leave anytime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. Call your doctor within the week to schedule your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted with a five-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the back and nonbloody emesis, consistent with an acute exacerbation. She was managed with bowel rest, TPN infusion via her existing PICC line, and symptom control using IV hydromorphone and ondansetron. Her pain and nausea gradually improved, allowing transition to oral medications and a soft diet by hospital day 6. She was started on oral vitamin B12 due to borderline low levels, and impacted cerumen was identified in the right ear, with instructions to avoid self-cleaning and follow up with her PCP or ENT. She was discharged home in stable condition with plans for close GI follow-up to manage TPN discontinuation, nutritional lab monitoring, and iron supplementation as an outpatient.
